title: Adaptive Batcher Impact: sequence-length cohort latency case study
body:
Summary:

This document captures a focused investigation into how the adaptive batcher affects end-to-end latency quantiles (p50/p95/p99) across sequence-length cohorts and cache warm/cold conditions. The adaptive batcher is the runtime component that dynamically selects a batching window based on observed QPS and target latency SLO. We ran controlled A/B runs comparing:

- Baseline: fixed-window batcher (20ms batch wait) with current production kernel selection.
- Adaptive: new adaptive batcher algorithm v2.1 (aggressively increases window under high QPS, decays quickly on tail signals).

Goals:
- Measure p50/p95/p99 E2E latency delta for representative routes.
- Produce per-stage breakdowns to identify where additional latency is introduced (or saved).
- Surface cohort-level regressions (short vs long prompts, cold vs warm KV).
- Recommend mitigations and telemetry to guardrails.

Test setup and dataset:
- Hardware: 8xA100-80GB cards per serving node, same instance class for both A/B.
- Model: open-llama-7B trimmed to production FP16 kernels + optimized attention kernels.
- Traffic shape: synthetic replay of production trace for a 30-minute window (mixed seqlen distribution: 40% 16-64 tokens, 40% 128-256 tokens, 20% 512-1024 tokens).
- QPS targets: steady 80% of node max throughput, and a separate 10-minute microburst at 120% to test overload fallbacks.
- KV cache warm/cold: toggled by flushing KV between runs to simulate first-request cold starts.
- Instrumentation: per-request trace includes timestamps for: recv, tokenize, preproc, batch_wait_start, batch_dispatch, model_forward_start, model_forward_finish, kv_lookup_start/finish, kv_write, postprocess, serialize, egress.

High-level results (aggregated):
- Baseline fixed-window:
  - p50: 68ms
  - p95: 210ms
  - p99: 480ms
- Adaptive batcher v2.1:
  - p50: 72ms (+6%)
  - p95: 190ms (-9.5%)
  - p99: 575ms (+19.8%)

Interpretation: adaptive batching reduced the mid-tail (p95) by shrinking effective batch waits during sustained periods of lower seqlen, yielding fewer small-batch inefficiencies. However, p99 regressed significantly — the tail became heavier, driven by a small population of traces that experienced long batch-window amplification during the microburst then hit queuing + slow kernel selection path. p50 increase is modest and traced primarily to slightly longer batching windows on short bursts when the algorithm probes.

Per-stage breakdown (median across negatively impacted p99 traces):
- recv -> tokenize: 6% of extra p99 latency (serialization overhead spikes for large inputs in microburst).
- batch_wait: 42% (primary contributor) — a subset of requests waited an extra 120–320ms due to adaptive window expansion when burst QPS hit inter-node aggregation thresholds.
- model_forward (including kernel selection + KV miss penalties): 28% — kernel fallback path triggered for large seqlen combos under high contention, plus KV cache cold misses added 30–80ms per request for affected traces.
- postprocess/serialize/egress: 10% — queuing effects at the egress thread during sustained bursts.
- misc (preproc, logging): 14% (includes overhead from trace logging at debug-level enabled in the run).

Cohort-level observations:
- Short prompts (16–64 tokens): p95 improved by ~25ms on adaptive; p99 worsened by 10–15% but affected only ~0.7% of short-prompt traces. Root cause: occasionally piggybacked onto longer-request batches when adaptive window briefly increased.
- Medium prompts (128–256 tokens): p95 improved ~20ms, p99 stable. Adaptive batcher mostly matched batch sizes to throughput profile here.
- Long prompts (512–1024 tokens): p95 marginally worse (~+12ms), p99 worse (~+25%) due to kernel path changes and larger memory pressure causing sporadic slowdowns and KV cold penalties.
- Cold KV runs: p99 impact magnified — cold misses explain ~35–50ms of added tail.

Trace archetypes identified for p99 regression (examples):
1) Microburst amplified batch window: a flurry of short requests arrives; adaptive controller sees high instantaneous QPS across a window and expands the wait to improve throughput; meanwhile a few long seqlen requests arrive and get batched with many shorter ones, triggering slow kernel selection and memory pressure -> long tail.
2) Inter-node aggregation delay: the adaptive controller coordinate uses approximate global QPS estimates; disagreement between nodes causes some nodes to attempt larger windows while others go small, leading to uneven batching and cross-node head-of-line blocking.
3) KV cold miss overlap: requests that are cold for KV are more likely to be queued into a growing batch; their longer model_forward time cascades into queue delay for subsequent requests.

Mitigations and short-term actions:
- Add cohort-aware batch gating: prevent long-seq requests (>512 tokens) from being co-batched with short requests unless the window is <20ms. (PR: linked_artifacts entry).
- Conservative adaptive floor: cap adaptive expansion to +25% above fixed-window for 30s after a detected microburst to avoid prolonged tail.
- KV prefetch hinting: if incoming request matches recent prompt hash patterns, pre-warm KV to reduce cold miss incidence.
- Trace sampling flag: disable debug-level global logging in production runs; use sampled traces (0.1–1%) to reduce trace-induced tail noise.

Longer-term design suggestions:
- Global coordination refinement: move from approximate cross-node signals to shard-aware signals that favor local batching decisions when inter-node variance exceeds threshold.
- Dynamic cohorting: categorize requests at the edge (short/medium/long) and route them through cohort-specific batchers with separate windows and kernel pools. This reduces kernel fallback churn and memory interference.
- Adaptive backpressure to egress/serialize: ensure egress threads can shed or reprioritize work when internal queues exceed latency thresholds.

Telemetry and alerts to add:
- New SLO guardrail: p99 increase >10% vs baseline for any cohort should open alert and auto-disable aggressive adaptive expansion.
- Per-stage p99 dashboards per cohort (batch_wait, model_forward, kv_miss, egress).
- Microburst detection metric: 1s and 5s QPS deltas that can flip safe-mode for batcher controllers.

Experiment follow-ups planned:
- Run with cohort-aware gating enabled and microburst floor applied; measure p50/p95/p99 over 24 hours of production replay. (Assigned: Miguel).
- Evaluate KV prefetch heuristics on a 10% traffic shadow. (Assigned: Priya).
- Microbenchmark kernel-selection latency under mixed batch composition to quantify fallback cost. (Assigned: Evan).

Notes/Questions: 
- We should confirm whether the adaptive controller's node-level signal includes queue-depth feedback or only recent dispatch rates. If queue depth is not used, it may explain expansion under transient spikes.
- Consider adding a boolean header from the router indicating "preferred cohort" so batcher can make immediate split decisions without content inspection.

Appendix: quick numbers from sampled trace set (10k traces):
- Fraction of traces that hit adaptive-induced long batch_wait (>200ms): 0.9%
- Among those, 68% contained at least one long-seq (>512) request.
- Kernel fallback frequency increased from 0.4% -> 1.5% during microburst in adaptive run.

Action log: 
- 2025-01-12: triggered initial experiment and collected traces (Aisha).
- 2025-01-15: reproduced p99 regression with microburst vs baseline; opened JIRA-1234 (Miguel assigned).
- 2025-01-20: drafted cohort gating PR (linked).
- 2025-02-03: review and plan next 24h replay (this doc).

If you're reviewing: please focus on the cohort gating proposal and microburst floor thresholds — both are low-risk and likely to reduce the observed tail without sacrificing the p95 benefit. Feedback especially welcome from SRE and the kernel team on kernel fallback costs and memory interference expectations.
